description.p: nailong is a lightweight Minecraft: Java Edition launcher written in Rust. Choose a Minecraft version and Fabric, NeoForge, Forge or vanilla, watch the install progress, and launch the game with an offline account. Incomplete downloads are detected and can be repaired.
It ships as a single native executable with no bundled runtime and keeps the launcher itself small.
Keyboard paths: Ctrl+1–4 switch primary pages, Ctrl+, opens Settings, F5 refreshes versions. Shortcuts yield to text fields and open dialogs, with a discoverable hint in Settings.

Settings polish: a 1 GB memory stepper replaces the raw DragValue, the Java row shows the actual runtime with Recheck and a download link when missing, and name/memory/Java no longer share one crowded line.

Update confirmation: “Update all” and single-row updates show a checklist with each project’s from → to version, target instance, download size, old-file cleanup and the automatic restore point before writing anything.

Control consistency: version statistics put the number above its label, Auto Backup and Show Base Versions use the warm toggle switch instead of default checkboxes, and the Saves toolbar is ordered auto-backup → interval → keep → back up all → prune.

Failure states and dismissal polish: a failed login opens a dedicated result card with Retry and Close, Escape closes Settings, Account, Restore Points, login wait and login error, and content errors offer Reload. Raw OAuth details stay in the Settings log.

Interaction fixes: Windows login links are opened without cmd so the full OAuth query survives, cancelling login no longer poisons content browsing, and Home/version summaries are cached per page with a shorter transition. Content shows a skeleton while loading, and login errors are short and actionable.

Loader-aware restore points: version JSON and patched client jar inside an isolated version directory are stored with the content restore point and restored exactly. Reinstalling or repairing an existing loader takes a point first. Shared libraries are not copied, and world saves keep their separate snapshot system.

Install confirmation and first-launch onboarding: every content install now shows the target version, destination directory, file, size, dependencies and a restore-point note before writing; cancelling leaves disk untouched. First launch becomes a three-step guide for Java 21+, the game directory, and installing the first version or importing a modpack.

Instance content restore points: mods, configs, resource packs, shaders and the content index are stored in a deduplicated object store, snapshotted automatically before installs, updates, imports and deletes. The Content page gains a restore-point dialog with manual creation, verified restore and a safety point of the current state. World saves keep their own separate snapshot system.

The play-first product pass: the home screen is rebuilt around a single primary action and a recent world, while account, memory, Java, paths and logs move into a sidebar Settings dialog with persisted preferences. Decorative status rings, dashboard cards and quick-action clutter are removed from Home.

Typography and control polish: a real bold CJK family for headings, list titles and primary buttons, a matte amber primary action with optional play/download glyphs, and layered secondary buttons with warm borders and contact shadows.

A warm cream, yellow and orange light theme replaces the dark UI. A persistent sidebar now holds four top-level places: Home, Versions, Content and Saves. Content merges discovery and installed items into one library with mode tabs, and Saves becomes a first-class page with its own version picker instead of a subpage of version management. Install and detail pages get explicit local back paths, and the layout is rechecked down to 900×620.

The design system gained light and motion: ambient glows and drifting embers, card hover lift with accent borders, a page-transition veil, a breathing gradient primary action, an animated progress bar with a moving sheen, and modal fade-ins.

The launcher UI was rebuilt around one design system: a warm accent on a dark neutral palette, a fixed page header with a single scrolling content area, consistent cards, list rows, switches, popovers and empty states. The download center gained a redesigned browsing grid, a project page with install/version panels, and a real content manager with filtering, update banners, per-row updates and inline delete confirmation. Main, install, version manager, saves, progress and the account/login dialogs were rebuilt as well, and the whole app is responsive down to 900×620.

World backups became git-style snapshots: content-defined chunking with a shared object store, so only changed chunks are stored. Snapshots can be restored or deleted, pruned by count, and scheduled automatically every 15–120 minutes.

Download center targets an installed version explicitly and writes into that version's folder, with a browse-only mode. Version management gains per-version content and saves pages: list worlds, back them up to zip, restore and delete, plus enable/disable and open-folder actions for mods and resource packs.
The loopback probe now recognises the login_required redirect as success instead of treating every AADSTS response as a rejection.
The login probe now follows the whole redirect chain, so a missing loopback redirect URI is reported with an actionable message instead of failing later in the browser.
Login now probes the loopback redirect URIs registered in Azure and uses the one Microsoft accepts (usually http://localhost), and accepts the callback on the root path.

Microsoft account login via browser authorization code + PKCE: the launcher opens the Microsoft page, catches the loopback callback, walks MSA → Xbox Live → XSTS → Minecraft Services, stores the refreshing token with 0600 permissions, and launches with the real access token. Offline mode is unchanged.

Browsing no longer forces a Minecraft version or loader: pick any version or “all versions” (all loaders) and browse the whole catalogue without installing anything first. Cards now show a short description.
Category chips are capped at twelve with a “more categories” toggle, so the browse header stays compact.
Only top-level CurseForge categories are shown as chips by default, keeping the browse header compact.
CurseForge categories are fetched at runtime and rendered as native chips, with a source switch for All / Modrinth / CurseForge. Downloads still go through the launcher with verification.

Browse-first download center: category chips, popular and newest shelves, icon cards and one-click install of the latest compatible release with required dependencies. Search moved to the top bar and now renders the same cards.

Complete download center: mod, resource-pack and shader search with pagination, dependency planning, installed-content index with enable/disable/delete, duplicate detection, update checks and local imports.
Mod discovery for Fabric, NeoForge and Forge: search Modrinth and CurseForge, choose a compatible file, review required/optional dependencies, and download into a version-isolated mods directory.

CurseForge credentials are now built in and lightly obfuscated; the user-facing API key setting and local settings file were removed. Maintainers can still override the key with an environment variable.

Official builds include a project CurseForge API key so regular users can import CurseForge packs without configuring one. Runtime environment variables and user settings still take precedence; the embedded key is extractable and treated as a shared default quota.
Install cancellation: downloads, extraction and loader processors now respond to a cancel button; completed parts are kept for the next repair.

CurseForge compliance fixes: respect files whose authors disabled third-party distribution, use the official download page instead of synthesizing CDN URLs, space out metadata requests, and support an optional build-time default key.

The settings page can store a CurseForge API key for official file metadata, size and SHA1 verification. The key is masked, written to the data directory with owner-only permissions on Unix, and never logged.
Modpack imports now cover Modrinth, CurseForge, Prism/MultiMC, MCBBS, HMCL and ATLauncher, with optional CurseForge API hashes.
Modpack imports: Modrinth .mrpack, CurseForge manifest zip and Prism/MultiMC exports, with format detection and loader installation.
Downloader upgrades: four-way range download for large single files, resumable segment parts, cross-source fallback, and a 180-second transfer timeout.
Content-addressed patched-client reuse: scan existing launcher roots, verify, and hardlink instead of downloading the patch or running processors.
Parallel install pipeline: assets, client/libraries, loader patch and processors now run concurrently where dependencies allow.
Size-optimized release (about 7.6 MB), a machine-wide patch cache, and the version management from 0.4.3.

Loader base versions are hidden from the main picker, with a management page for deleting versions and instances. Reinstalling an intact loader is now instant, and the 3 MB core data is fetched in parallel.
Forge and NeoForge installs now fetch only the core installer data (about 3 MB) instead of the full 7–9 MB package; mirrors without range support fall back safely.
Fabric, NeoForge, Forge and vanilla installs, with version pickers, progress and repair.
